summary: German numbers are built like a kit. 0–12 are single words (null, eins, zwei … elf, zwölf); 13–19 are unit + zehn (dreizehn, vierzehn); the tens end in -zig (zwanzig, vierzig … neunzig – but dreißig with ß); then hundert and tausend. Between the tens German says the unit first, joined with und, all in one word: 21 = einundzwanzig (“one-and-twenty”), 45 = fünfundvierzig. Watch three short cuts: sechzehn and sechzig drop the s of sechs, siebzehn and siebzig drop the -en of sieben. Counting, you say eins; before a noun the number one is the article ein / eine / ein with its endings – in everyday German the only number that changes its form (rare old forms like zweier, dreier aside). After zwei and above the noun is plural: zwei Stühle, zehn Kinder. Amounts without a number: viel / viele (much / many), wenig / wenige (little / few), ein bisschen / ein wenig (a little), alle (all), einige / manche (some): the forms without -e go with a singular uncountable noun (viel Papier), the forms with -e with a plural (viele Bücher). Age is said with sein: Ich bin achtzehn.

blocks.title: eins or ein?
blocks.text: eins is the number standing alone: Eins, zwei, drei! · Eins und eins ist zwei. Before a noun the number “one” is the article: ein Stuhl, eine Tasse, ein Buch (and einen Stuhl in the accusative). In compounds: einundzwanzig (no s), but hunderteins (with s).

blocks.title: zwo
blocks.text: zwei and drei sound alike on a bad line, so on the phone, on the radio and in the army Germans say zwo. It is the old feminine form of “two” and is perfectly correct in speech.

blocks.title: Age: sein, not haben
blocks.text: Ich bin achtzehn (Jahre alt). – I am eighteen. Never *Ich habe achtzehn: German, like Greek, English and Turkish, uses “to be” for age.

blocks.title: Points and commas
blocks.text: German writes 1.000 for a thousand and 1,5 for one and a half – the opposite of English. 2,50 € = zwei Euro fünfzig.

items.title: The noun after a number
points: German: plural from zwei on (zwei Stühle) – as in Greek and English
Turkish keeps the singular (iki sandalye); Russian changes the case (два стула, пять стульев)

askYourself: Am I counting or naming the number alone? → eins. Is it before a noun? → ein / eine / ein with endings.
Is it 13–19? → unit + zehn; careful with sechzehn and siebzehn.
Is it a round ten? → -zig (dreißig with ß; sechzig, siebzig shortened).
Is it between two tens? → unit + und + ten, one word: dreiundvierzig. Does the unit keep its full form? Yes: sechsundzwanzig, siebenundzwanzig.
Is the number 2 or more? → the noun goes in the plural: zwei Stühle.
Is the noun uncountable (Papier, Zeit) or plural (Bücher)? → viel / wenig or viele / wenige.
Am I saying someone’s age? → sein: Ich bin zwanzig.
steps: Find the unit and the ten.
Say the unit first, then und, then the ten.
Put the noun in the plural after 2 or more.

traps: sechzehn, sechzig (no s) – but sechsundzwanzig (with s).
dreißig is the only ten with -ßig.
The noun after a number above one is plural: zwei Bücher, not *zwei Buch (Turkish speakers beware: iki kitap).
viel / wenig with an uncountable singular, viele / wenige with a plural: viel Papier, viele Stühle.
Age with sein: Ich bin fünfzehn, not *Ich habe fünfzehn.

quiz.why: The unit first, then und, then the ten – and ein without s.
sechzehn drops the s of sechs; sechzig is 60.
siebzig drops the -en of sieben; siebzehn is 17.
The only ten with -ßig; dreizehn is 13.
Before a noun “one” is the article ein (masculine nominative); eins only stands alone.
After zwei the noun is plural: der Stuhl – die Stühle.
Papier is an uncountable singular here: viel, no ending.

quiz.q: Why do Germans often say zwo on the phone?
options: so that it is not confused with drei
because it is the plural of zwei
quiz.answer: so that it is not confused with drei
quiz.why: zwei and drei sound alike; zwo is the old feminine form of two.
Age is said with sein in German.

seeAlso.note: Arabic also says the units first (wāḥid wa-ʿišrūn, “one and twenty”), but 3–10 take the opposite gender of the noun, and after 11–99 the noun is singular.
Hebrew numbers come in a masculine and a feminine set and say the tens first (עֶשְׂרִים וְאֶחָד, twenty and one).
Chinese numbers are perfectly regular (十一, 二十一) but need a measure word before the noun (三本书); before a measure word 两 replaces 二.
After zwei and above the German noun is plural – learn each noun with its plural.
